description.narrative:
"Project Summary
The NIHR STOP-HBV project is a multi-country global health research programme funded by the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) and led by Imperial College London. The project aims to strengthen hepatitis B virus (HBV) prevention, diagnosis, and care pathways in sub-Saharan Africa, contributing to progress towards WHO hepatitis elimination targets.
HBV remains a major cause of liver cirrhosis and liver cancer in Africa, with limited access to systematic screening, laboratory monitoring, and long-term antiviral treatment. STOP-HBV addresses these gaps through implementation research embedded within routine health systems. The project combines clinical research, laboratory strengthening, capacity building, and policy translation to develop scalable and sustainable models of care.
The programme focuses on improving: • Identification of pregnant women and adults living with chronic HBV • Linkage to specialist liver care • Access to antiviral treatment • Monitoring of liver disease progression • Integration of HBV services within national health systems
The project also strengthens local research capacity through training of PhD students, project managers, and clinical researchers, and supports institutional governance and data management systems.
Countries Involved and Specific Roles:
United Kingdom Imperial College London (Lead Contractor and Sponsor) Imperial College London leads and coordinates the overall project. Responsibilities include: • Scientific leadership (Chief Investigator: Prof. Maud Lemoine) • Overall project governance and management • Sponsor responsibilities and regulatory oversight • Central financial management • Contracts and partner agreements The Gambia MRC Unit The Gambia at the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine (LSHTM) The Gambia site hosts the West African implementation component of STOP-HBV. Responsibilities include: • Participant recruitment and follow-up within antenatal and clinical services • Delivery of HBV screening and clinical management • Laboratory testing (virology and liver disease assessment) • Local data collection and management • Engagement with the Ministry of Health for translation into policy • Contribution to scientific outputs and dissemination University of Liverpool (UK) The University of Liverpool collaborates through its long-standing partnership with MLW. Responsibilities include: • Academic oversight and co-investigator input • Clinical research leadership in Malawi (Dr Alexander Stockdale and collaborators) • Data analysis and interpretation • Contribution to publications and capacity building
United Kingdom Canterbury Christ Church University (CCCU) • Implementation science and public health expertise • Support for evaluation methodology and health systems analysis • Contribution to capacity building and training activities • Participation in dissemination and knowledge translation CCCU contributes academic expertise but does not hold ownership of in-country Research Data.
Malawi Kamuzu University of Health Sciences (KUHeS) • National academic partner in Malawi • Integration of research within medical education and health workforce development • Clinical collaboration through QECH • Strengthening institutional research capacity • Contribution to sustainability and translation into national policy
Coolaborators do also include: Malawi Liverpool Wellcome Programme (MLW) Governmental health facilities The Gambia Young Gambian Fund, The Gambia World Hepatitis Alliance
• Host institution for Malawi implementation site • Embedded within Queen Elizabeth Central Hospital (QECH), Blantyre • Recruitment and follow-up of pregnant women • Laboratory diagnostics and viral load monitoring • Implementation research and community engagement • Local regulatory compliance and governance
"
